Of the 92 notice-less major rules that invoked the good-cause exception, 36 
rules involved a looming (or already-past) statutory deadline; 31 involved 
a statute that prescribed the content of the rule; and 19 involved an 
emergency (note these categories overlapped).
A common reason for an agency to consider notice and comment 
‘‘unnecessary” is that the rule is likely to be uncontroversial. When an 
agency thinks a rule will be uncontroversial, it may engage in direct final 
rulemaking, that is, promulgate the rule with the proviso that the agency 
will withdraw it—and proceed with full-blown notice and comment—if it 
receives any adverse comment within a certain period. This practice is not 
expressly authorized by the APA; it is a way to operationalize the exception 
for when notice and comment is “unnecessary.”
If an agency correctly concludes that notice and comment would be 
“impracticable” or “contrary to pubhc interest” (e.g., because of a deadline 
or emergency), then the agency is, in principle, free to promulgate a rule 
without any sohcitation of comment at all. In fact, however, an agency often 
invokes this exception and then announces that, as a matter of grace, it 
will (1) receive and consider comments while the rule remains in effect and 
(2) revise or withdraw the rule if the comments persuade it to do so. This 
technique is called interim final rulemaking, since the rule remains in 
effect as an interim measure while the agency voluntarily receives and 
considers comments (though the rule may end up being permanent if the 
agency opts not to act on the comments). Though receiving comments is 
officially a matter of grace, the agency actually has a hard incentive to do 
so: agencies find it easier to convince reviewing courts that pre-
promulgation notice and comment was “impracticable” or “contrary to 
pubhc interest” than that any notice and comment was such. Michael 
Asimow, Interim-Final Rules: Making Haste Slowly, 51 Ad min . L. Re v . 703, 
723-24 (1999).
By the 2010s, interim final rulemaking was resulting in scenarios 
where (1) the agency invoked good cause to impose an IFR without notice 
and comment, (2) the agency took comment after imposing the IFR, and (3) 
the agency, after receiving the comments, promulgated a final rule. In this 
situation, the final rule could be quite similar to the IFR, and the agency’s 
justification for invoking good cause to forego notice and comment on the 
IFR might have been doubtful. In that situation, what should a reviewing 
court do with the final rule?
